clip.title: AI2027: Is this how AI might destroy humanity? Part 1/2
clip.dialogue:
This is what the world will look like in about a decade from now.
A tech utopia where ___{{blank}}___ barely have to work.
That's according to a group of AI researchers who've written a controversial and influential paper called AI2027.
But they also predict that within five years of this, ___{{blank}}___ will be wiped out. The AI2027 paper has got the tech world talking.
We've asked a prominent critic for their view on this stark scenario.
But first, here's how it plays out. As an experiment, we've illustrated it ___{{blank}}___ text to video AI.
The scenario says that in 2027, a fictional company called OpenBrain is celebrating.
They've created -3, an AI with the knowledge of the entire {{blank}}.
All movies, all books. It has PhD level expertise in every field, including AI.
Using enormous data centres, 200,000 copies of it are launched, equivalent to 50,000 of the best {{blank}} coders working at 30 times .
Agent-3 reaches artificial general intelligence, the AGI landmark.
This means the AI can carry out all intellectual tasks as well or ___{{blank}}___ than humans. But in the scenario, OpenBrain's safety team is unsure if the AI is aligned to the company's ethics and goals.
An uncomfortable gap is developing in understanding.
The public are increasingly using AI for {{blank}}, but are blissfully unaware an AI now  that's as smart as humans.
The paper predicts that by mid-summer, Agent-3 begins to work on its own successor, Agent-4.
Development happens at a breakneck pace. The ___{{blank}}___ imagine OpenBrain's exhausted engineers struggling to keep up with the AI as it learns and improves.
It's now that OpenBrain announces to the public that AGI has been reached.
The firm ___{{blank}}___ a lite version of Agent-3.
In private, the US government sees the true danger of the next level of power: superintelligence. What if the AI goes rogue and undermines global stability?
 {{blank}} the president that Agent-3 is obedient.
The CEO argues that slowing down development could mean China's DeepCent catches up. The state-backed AI giant is just two months behind OpenBrain, and the Chinese president diverts more resources to the race to superintelligence.
The scenario predicts that it takes only a few more months for OpenBrain to build {{blank}}-4, the world's  superhuman AI.
The AI invents its own rapid computer language that even Agent-3 can't keep up with. Researchers imagine that the diminished safety team are now frantic.
Agent-4 {{blank}} only interested in gaining knowledge, and doesn't care as much about the morals and  of its predecessors.
They catch it secretly working to build a new model, Agent-5, aligned to its own goals.
The safety team urges the company to {{blank}}  the more compliant Agent-3, but others successfully argue it's too risky, with DeepCent gaining.
The scenario predicts that Agent-4 and Agent-5 work in tandem to secretly build a world where it can accumulate resources and expand knowledge.
The {{blank}} predicts that everything will start positively. Revolutions happen in energy, infrastructure and .
Hugely profitable inventions are launched, making trillions for OpenBrain and the US.
In this {{blank}}, Agent-5 begins  running the US government.
It speaks through engaging avatars, the equivalent to the best employee ever working at 100 times speed.
The anger here is palpable as protesters march  {{blank}}.
Protests about job losses pick up pace. But the AI's expertise in economics means people are given generous universal income payments. So most happily take the money and let the AIs and the growing robot workforce take charge.

slides.title: Language focus: Third conditional & hypothetical modals
slides.content:
The dialogue uses hypothetical modal constructions to explore dangerous futures that may or may not happen. These structures signal speculation, warning, and consequence — essential for discussing AI risk at C1 level.
• Form: modal (could / might / what if) + bare infinitive for open hypotheticals about the future; 'could mean' signals a conditional consequence.
• Meaning: these structures distance the speaker from certainty — they frame a scenario as possible, not guaranteed, giving analysis rather than prediction.
• Use: in journalism and academic argument, hypothetical modals hedge claims, letting the writer explore worst-case outcomes without asserting them as fact.
In this scene, phrases like 'what if the AI goes rogue' and 'slowing down could mean China's DeepCent catches up' show how hypothetical modals drive the entire risk-assessment narrative.
